title: Use built-in Fabric data protection to get your data AI-ready
summary: A Fabric Updates Blog post from the Power BI team framing what it means for an organization's data estate to be safely exposed to Copilot and agentic AI, then mapping that framing onto the Purview-integrated protection controls already built into Fabric: sensitivity labels, protection policies, DLP, DLP restrict access, and Purview DSPM for Fabric.
audience: Fabric security admins, data governance leads, and platform architects who are being asked to open lakehouses, warehouses, and semantic models to Copilot or custom agents without losing control over who can see what.
why_it_matters: As agent- and Copilot-style consumption spreads across a tenant, oversharing risk scales with it, so architects need a concrete checklist mapping classification, access control, protection persistence, and auditability to the specific Fabric/Purview features that implement each, rather than treating 'AI-ready' as only a data-quality concern.
takeaways: AI-readiness from a security standpoint is framed as four questions: what sensitive data exists, where it lives, who can access it, and how it's protected/observed.
The same Purview sensitivity labels used across Microsoft 365 extend into Fabric items and Power BI content, with protection following the data on export.
Protection policies and DLP restrict-access are the enforcement mechanisms that actually narrow who an agent's queries can reach, since agents operate under the querying user's own permissions.
DSPM for Fabric adds a posture-management layer that surfaces overshared or unlabeled assets and AI-usage risk signals, rather than just static classification.
The article stitches these together as a five-step adoption sequence rather than presenting them as independent, unrelated features.

claims.text: Sensitivity labels defined in Microsoft Purview Information Protection can be applied to Fabric items and Power BI content using the same labeling taxonomy already used across Microsoft 365, either manually, by default, or via a mandatory labeling policy.

A sensitivity label's protection travels with the underlying data: when labeled Fabric or Power BI content is exported to Excel, PowerPoint, PDF, or .pbix, encryption is enforced so only authorized users can open the exported file.

Protection policies are tied to a specific sensitivity label and restrict access to any item carrying that label to a named set of users and groups, blocking everyone else; this is supported for native Fabric items and Power BI semantic models.

Purview Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies scoped to Fabric and Power BI workspaces automatically detect sensitive information types and labels in semantic models and OneLake structured items such as lakehouses, SQL databases, mirrored databases, and KQL databases, and can be run first in simulation mode to tune detection before enforcement.

DLP restrict access is a preview enforcement action that automatically limits who can reach an item matched by a DLP policy, ranging from blocking external users to restricting access to admins only in higher-sensitivity cases.

A Protect, secure, and comply report inside the OneLake Catalog's Govern tab shows tenant-wide sensitivity label coverage, and audit logs separately track label activity and DLP detections for ongoing visibility.

Microsoft Purview Data Security Posture Management (DSPM) for Fabric discovers data risks such as sensitive data appearing in AI prompts and responses, and runs Data Risk Assessments that identify overshared, unprotected, or sensitive Fabric assets so admins can target remediation like applying labels or policies.

Because agents and Copilot operate within the querying user's own permissions rather than a separate service identity, tightening access controls on the underlying data directly constrains what an AI experience can retrieve and surface, without any AI-specific configuration.
